lit-0079: Think of two ways a village elder might praise a strong young man: 'He fights like a lion' versus 'He is a lion in battle.' Do both sentences use the exact same wording structure, or is there a small but noticeable difference in how directly each one states the comparison?

Exactly the structural difference. Given that one explicitly signals the comparison with a word like 'like' or 'as', while the other states the comparison directly as if it were literally true, which one would you call a simile, and which a metaphor?
lit-0001: Good question. Before I tell you — think about when your mother says 'this yam is stubborn, it refuses to get soft.' Can a yam actually refuse anything?
Exactly that idea. So if the yam can't really 'refuse', what is the writer doing when they say the sun 'refused' to rise?
That's it — that's called personification. Now, why might a poet choose to say the sun 'refused' rather than simply 'the sun did not rise'? What mood does 'refused' add?
lit-0015: When your aunty says 'I have warned you a thousand times not to play near that gutter', has she actually counted a thousand warnings, or is she making a point some other way?

Exactly — she's exaggerating on purpose for effect, not stating a fact. So back in the play, is 'a million times' meant to be counted literally, or is it doing the same job as your aunty's 'a thousand times'?
Right — what's the specific literary term for deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis rather than literal truth, and what emotion is it emphasising here?
lit-0034: Think of a naming ceremony where the grandmother is dancing and singing with the guests, but also quietly weeping because the baby is named after her late husband. Can real feelings actually be that mixed, joy and grief together, in the same moment?

Good. So when a poet deliberately puts two opposite words side by side — 'joyful' and 'mourning' — is that a mistake, or a compressed way of capturing exactly that kind of real, contradictory emotion?

Right — what is the specific term for a figure of speech that combines two contradictory terms for effect, and what mixed emotional truth about the wedding might it be pointing to here — perhaps a bride leaving her family home?
lit-0111: Let's look closely at the relationship in each case. Is a 'crown' literally a PART of the king's body, the way a 'hand' is literally a PART of a worker's body?

No wahala, let's narrow it down: when you substitute something CLOSELY ASSOCIATED with a thing (but not literally part of it) to represent that thing — like 'the crown' standing for 'the king/monarchy' — that's METONYMY. When you use an actual PART of something to represent the WHOLE (or the whole to represent a part) — like 'hands' (a body part) standing for whole workers/people — that's SYNECDOCHE. Given that distinction, which term applies to 'the crown will decide', and which to 'all hands were needed'?

You've correctly matched both — well reasoned. Let's confirm fully: METONYMY substitutes a closely ASSOCIATED term for the thing itself without a part-whole relationship (crown = monarchy/kingship, by association). SYNECDOCHE specifically uses a PART to represent the WHOLE, or occasionally the whole to represent a part (hands = whole people, since a hand is literally a body part of each worker). The key test is always: is the substituted term an actual physical part of the thing (synecdoche), or merely something associated with it (metonymy)?
lit-0029: Say the word 'clang' out loud slowly. Does it just describe a metal sound, or does saying it actually sound a bit like metal striking metal?

Exactly — the word's sound imitates the thing it describes. Compare that to if the poet had instead written 'the hammer made a noise' — would that give you the same immediate sensory experience of being at the blacksmith's forge?
Right — so what is the specific term for words whose sound imitates the sound they describe, and what effect does it have on the reader's experience of the scene at the forge?
lit-0009: Think of a talking drum player at a festival — he doesn't just hit the drum randomly, he repeats a particular beat pattern to build a mood, maybe heaviness for mourning or urgency for war. Does the repeated pattern serve the mood, or is it just noise?
Right. Now say 'silent, sullen, suffering slaves' slowly to yourself — that repeated hard 's' sound — does it come out sounding light and quick, or heavy and drawn-out, almost like a hiss or a groan?
So if the repeated 's' sound physically forces the reader to slow down and produce something like a hiss or sigh, what mood or feeling about the slaves' condition might that sound be reinforcing?
lit-0049: Think of how 'moon' and 'lagoon' actually do rhyme fully at the end, but notice the word 'swoons' in the middle also shares that same 'oo' sound, even though it doesn't rhyme with anything at a line's end here. Is a shared vowel sound INSIDE a line the same as two words rhyming at the ends of separate lines?

Good distinction. Rhyme usually refers to matching end sounds across line endings, while a repeated vowel sound running through words within or across a line, without needing matching consonants after it, has its own separate name. Do you recall what that's called?
That's the correct term. So what musical or unifying effect might repeating that soft 'oo' sound across 'moon', 'swoons' and 'lagoon' have on how the line feels when read aloud?
lit-0064: Think of a political rally speaker who begins sentence after sentence with 'We will rebuild...', 'We will restore...', 'We will reclaim...'. Does repeating that same opening phrase make the speech feel weaker and more repetitive, or does it build momentum and conviction as it continues?

Exactly — repeated openings can build rhetorical force. Now in the poem's second stanza, does repeating 'We shall...' at the start of each line seem to build a similar mounting determination or resolve as the stanza progresses?
Good. What is the specific term for this device — repeating the same word or phrase at the START of successive lines — and how does it serve the stanza's overall tone of resolve?
lit-0054: Think of a native flute player who doesn't pause cleanly between musical phrases but lets one note bleed straight into the next, no clean breaks. Does that create a sense of smooth continuous flow, or does it sound broken and accidental?

Good parallel. Now, when a poetic line runs on into the next without a pause or punctuation, forcing you to read quickly onward to complete the thought, is that likely a printing accident, or a deliberate pacing choice by the poet?

Right — what is the technical term for a line running on into the next without a pause, and what effect might it create — urgency, breathlessness, or continuous flowing thought — at the specific point it occurs in this poem?
lit-0135: Think of school assembly. Before anything starts, the prefect shouts 'Assembly, attention!' and everyone stands straight. What does that call do before the announcements begin?
Exactly. Now in a moonlight tale in Yoruba land, the teller calls 'Alo o!' and the listeners reply 'Alo!' What do both sides show by that exchange?

Well put. These are called opening formulae, and many tales also have closing formulae. What would a closing formula do for the audience, and why might these formulae matter in oral performance more than in a written book?
lit-0136: Think of a church or mosque choir, or a football chant at the stadium. The leader shouts 'Super Eagles!' and the crowd replies 'Ooo-ooo!' What happens to the crowd when they reply together?

Right. So the pattern isn't just repeating words; it's about who is speaking. In the poem, one voice calls and a group answers. What does that tell you about the relationship between the leader and the community?
That's the heart of it: this is called call-and-response, a key feature of African oral poetry and song. How would that structure affect the mood of the poem when it's performed aloud?
lit-0137: Consider an age-grade meeting where a young member wants to collect the dues early. Instead of arguing, an elder says, 'The child who says his mother will not sleep will also not sleep.' Everyone goes quiet and nods. Why did the proverb win the argument better than a long explanation?
That's the key: authority, plus indirectness. Achebe's famous line calls proverbs the palm oil with which words are eaten. What does palm oil do to food, and what then do proverbs do to speech?
Exactly. So in your answer, what two or three things does the elder's use of proverbs achieve, and what does it tell us about him as a character and about the society?
lit-0134: Let's try this. Picture that one friend in your class who always finds a smart way to dodge punishment, like convincing the teacher that the whole class did the assignment. Do students admire him, or condemn him?

No wahala, let's pin it down. The class laughs at his smartness AND is happy when he finally gets caught. The tortoise stories work the same way: we enjoy his cleverness while the ending often punishes his greed. So, can the answer be only 'good' or only 'bad'?

Let's work it through together. Point 1: the tortoise is admired for intelligence, wit and survival skills; he's small but defeats the powerful, which delights the audience. Point 2: he's also greedy, selfish and deceitful, and many tales end with his punishment (e.g. the story explaining his cracked shell). Point 3: this double attitude is the essence of the trickster: he entertains while teaching that cleverness without honesty leads to downfall. So your thesis could be: 'The tortoise is an ambivalent trickster whom the tales both celebrate for wit and punish for greed.'
lit-0143: Let's think about a burial you've attended. When the women sing and cry, they often praise the dead person too. But is the main feeling in their song joy or grief?

Alright, let me narrow it. Praise poetry celebrates a living person's greatness. This poem praises someone who has DIED and keeps asking who will fill the gap they left. A song of mourning sung at burials has a specific name. Can you remember the word that starts with 'd'?

Yes, let's confirm it. Step 1: a dirge is a song or poem of lament for the dead, performed at funerals. Step 2: its features include mourning tone, direct address to the dead, questions about the loss ('who will now feed the goats?'), praise of the dead person's qualities, and often repetition. Step 3: the praise inside it serves the grief: it shows what the community has lost. So you'd write: 'This is a dirge, because it laments the dead, asks rhetorical questions about the loss, and recalls the person's virtues in a sorrowful tone.'
lit-0019: When your friend's danfo breaks down in traffic during rain and he laughs and says 'ah, today is my lucky day o', does he actually mean the day is lucky?

Exactly — saying the opposite of what is meant, usually for a bitter or humorous effect. Is 'sarcasm' just an everyday word for a feeling, or is there a specific literary term for this technique of saying the opposite of what's meant?

It's closely related to irony — specifically the kind that happens through what a character SAYS rather than through events. Given that clue, what would you call this device, and what does it reveal about the shop owner's emotional state in that moment?
lit-0011: Think of a man who buys the strongest padlock in the market to protect his shop from armed robbers, only to later discover his own trusted shop assistant has been taking money quietly all along. Is the danger he prepared for the same as the danger that actually got him?

Right — there's a gap between what he expected and what actually happened, from the exact place he thought was safe. Now, is 'irony' just any surprising twist, or specifically this kind of gap between expectation and outcome?

Good instinct — so with the father and his son, what makes this situational irony rather than a plain plot twist: is it merely that we didn't expect it, or is it that the outcome directly contradicts the very thing he tried to prevent?
lit-0004: Imagine you're watching a Nollywood film where the audience already saw the armed robbers hiding behind the house, but the security man on screen is whistling happily, telling his wife on the phone that all is quiet. Who knows more at that moment — the audience or the security man?
Right. Now apply that to the watchman's line — does the audience/reader already have information (maybe from an earlier scene) that makes his confidence sound hollow or even a little frightening?

So when a character speaks with confidence that the audience knows is misplaced, because we've been shown something they haven't, what literary device is at work, and what effect does it create — comedy, tension, or foreboding?
lit-0187: Think of a comedian doing a skit about a governor who commissions the same borehole three times. What is the comedian's aim with the whole skit?

Alright, let me narrow it. The comedian wants laughter, yes, but also to expose and criticise the governor's corruption. That whole purpose, ridiculing to criticise, is satire. Now, if in the skit the governor says 'I am a man of the people' while drinking champagne, what device is that single moment?

Let's work it through. Step 1: satire is a mode or purpose: using humour, exaggeration and ridicule to expose and criticise vice or folly, usually to encourage reform. Step 2: irony is one tool satire uses, along with exaggeration, caricature and parody. Step 3: so in your answer, say what the playwright satirises (e.g. corrupt politicians), then show the tools: ironic statements, exaggerated characters, absurd situations. Irony is part of the satire, not the same thing.
lit-0189: Think about a mother who finds her son's broken phone screen and asks calmly: 'Ah, what happened to this phone? Did it fall by itself?' Is she really confused?
Exactly. So the old woman's 'I'm just an old woman' is a performance. What do her simple questions force the councillor to do in front of everyone?
Right. Pretending ignorance to expose someone is sometimes called Socratic irony. What does this technique reveal about her character, and why is it more effective than openly accusing him?
lit-0068: Think about a village storyteller at night who pauses the story to speak directly to the listeners gathered round the fire, sharing his own private thoughts about what a character is secretly planning, even though no one 'in the story' can hear him say it. Is he breaking the story, or letting the audience in on something private?

Exactly that function. When a character speaks alone on stage, revealing his private thoughts, motives, or conflicts directly to the audience without other characters hearing, what do we call that dramatic device?
lit-0069: Think of two friends at a noisy naming ceremony — one leans slightly away and murmurs a private joke just for the person right beside them, quietly enough that the rest of the crowded room carries on as if nothing was said. Was anything actually wrong with the room not reacting, or is that murmur meant only for one listener?

Right idea, but on stage this device works slightly differently: it's meant for the AUDIENCE to hear, not the other characters, who conventionally do not react because they are understood not to hear it at all. What is this device called, where a character's remark is heard by the audience but treated as unheard by the other characters present?
lit-0072: Think about a long, tense village court case where accusations are flying and tempers are high, and then someone's goat wanders in and causes a bit of comic chaos, making everyone briefly laugh before the serious matter continues. Does that brief laughter erase the seriousness of the court case, or does it give everyone a short breather before the tension continues?

Exactly the function. When a playwright deliberately inserts a lighter, humorous moment into an otherwise tense or serious scene, giving the audience emotional relief before the tension resumes (and sometimes commenting on the main action from a different angle), what do we call this technique?
lit-0077: Think about a market woman who, early in the morning, quietly counts a hidden pouch of extra money under her wrapper before anyone else arrives, though nothing seems to come of it yet that day. If later in the story that hidden money becomes important — maybe she uses it to secretly bail out a relative — would that early detail have been pointless, or was it planting something for later?

Exactly the technique. When a playwright includes an early detail (an object, a gesture, a stage direction) that seems minor at first but sets up or hints at something significant that will matter later in the plot, what do we call this device?
lit-0174: Think of a Nollywood story where a rich man throws his poor brother out. Later, the man loses everything in a fire. Separately, in the final scene, he finds out that the brother he rejected was the one secretly paying his hospital bills. Are those two moments the same?
Good. So one is a change of fortune, the other is a change from ignorance to knowledge. Which Greek terms match which?
Right. They often happen close together, but they're different. In your play, can you identify each, and explain why the recognition often makes the reversal more painful?
lit-0150: Think about a Nollywood actor who plays a wicked stepmother. When she says 'I will destroy this family!', is the actress herself planning to destroy a family?
Right. Poets can do the same: create a voice that is not their own. In your poem, what kind of person seems to be speaking, based on what they say and do?
Good. That created voice is called the speaker or persona. Why might a poet choose to speak through a persona like this, rather than in their own voice?
lit-0163: Think of a comedian at a burial who speaks with gentle humour about the dead man's funny habits. Is the comedian's attitude the same as the overall feeling in the room?
Good. So one is the speaker's attitude, the other is the atmosphere created for the audience. Which is which?
Exactly. Now apply it to your poem, which describes a flooded street with sarcastic lines about the government's 'excellent drainage'. What's the tone, and what's the mood?
lit-0152: Think about a family WhatsApp group on someone's wedding day. It starts with pictures and 'Congratulations!' Then suddenly someone posts: 'But where is the groom's father? Has anybody heard from him since morning?' What happens to the mood of the group chat?
Right. So look at your poem again. Is there a word or line where the direction changes, like that 'But' in the group chat?
Great spotting. So how would you describe the tone of the whole poem now, and why might the poet set up joy first before turning?
lit-0154: Think of a pastor's sermon or an imam's lesson. He builds his message in three sections, and then at the end he says 'In summary, brethren...' and gives one sharp line people will remember. What is that last line for?
Right. Sometimes that closing line also surprises you. Look at your sonnet: the three quatrains praise the beauty of the harmattan morning. What do the last two lines say?
So here the couplet does more than summarise. This form, three quatrains and a couplet, is the Shakespearean (English) sonnet. What is the effect of placing that twist in the final couplet?
lit-0160: Think of that uncle at a family gathering who keeps saying 'I'm a very humble man, the humblest in this family', while ordering everyone around. What does his behaviour tell you, versus his words?

Okay, narrower. Look at the details the landlord mentions by accident: he threw the last tenant's things into the rain, he raised rent twice in one year, and he calls it 'generosity'. Is the poem asking us to believe him, or to notice the gap between what he says and what he did?

Let's work through it. Step 1: a poem in which a single speaker addresses a silent listener at a key moment is a dramatic monologue. Step 2: the key feature is that the speaker reveals his character unintentionally; his own details betray him. Step 3: here the landlord's boasting about generosity is undercut by his harsh actions, creating irony and exposing him as greedy and cruel. So: 'The dramatic monologue lets the landlord condemn himself; his claims of generosity are ironically contradicted by the details he reveals.'
phy-0001: Think of an okada braking to stop at a checkpoint. At the start it is moving fast, and at the end, how fast is it moving when it has fully stopped?
Good — so 'comes to rest' means final velocity v = 0 m/s. Now, out of u, v, a, t — which three values do you already know from the question?
Exactly right. Now which of the standard equations of motion has only u, v, a and t in it, with no distance s?
Correct formula. Now rearrange it to make a the subject, then substitute your three known values — what do you get?
phy-0026: Think of two market women walking toward each other from opposite ends of a long road, one walking briskly and one walking more slowly. Is the gap between them closing faster than either woman's own walking speed alone, or slower?

Exactly — when two things move toward each other, their approach speeds combine because both contribute to closing the same distance. Now, would that same addition logic apply if the two buses were instead moving in the SAME direction, one chasing the other?

Right distinction — direction determines add or subtract for relative velocity. So back to our two buses moving toward each other at 15 m/s and 10 m/s, using vec(v) as vectors in opposite directions, what is their relative velocity of approach?
phy-0002: Think of a mango falling from a tree branch when nobody throws it, it just lets go. At the very instant it leaves the branch, is it already moving fast, or is it starting from rest?
Exactly — 'dropped' always means initial velocity u = 0 m/s. Now, which equation of motion relates distance s to u, a (which is g here) and t, without needing final velocity v?
Correct choice. Now substitute u = 0 m/s, a = g = 10 m/s^2, and t = 3 s into that formula — what expression do you get before you finish the arithmetic?
phy-0009: Let's slow down and check what we actually have first, like a trader counting her wares before pricing them. From the question, which of u, v, a, t, s do you already know?

No wahala, here's a strong hint: out of the standard equations of motion, only one connects u, v, a and s together with no t in it at all — it looks like v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s. Try substituting your three known values into that one and see what you can isolate for a.
Let's work through it together step by step: v^2 = u^2 + 2*a*s becomes 12^2 = 4^2 + 2*a*32, which is 144 = 16 + 64*a. Subtracting 16 from both sides gives 128 = 64*a, so a = 128/64 = 2 m/s^2.
phy-0108: Think of a market woman who tosses an orange sideways off a high balcony at the exact same moment her friend simply drops another orange straight down from the same height. Which orange do you think reaches the ground first — the tossed one or the dropped one?

Let's narrow it down: in projectile motion, the horizontal motion (sideways) and vertical motion (falling) act completely independently of each other — the sideways push does NOT affect how fast gravity pulls it down. So actually, both oranges hit the ground at the SAME time. Given that, which of the standard equations of motion should you use to find the time to fall, using only the VERTICAL drop height and treating initial vertical velocity as zero?

Good formula choice, let's solve it together: with u = 0 (no initial vertical velocity), s = 0.5*a*t^2 simplifies to s = 0.5*g*t^2. Rearranging for t: t = sqrt(2*s/g). Substituting s = 45 m and g = 10 m/s^2: t = sqrt(2*45/10) = sqrt(9) = 3 s. So the stone takes 3 seconds to hit the ground, regardless of how fast it was thrown horizontally.
phy-0011: Let's reason it out first. Think of a line of dancers doing a Bata dance step, where each dancer repeats the same movement 50 times in one minute, and each complete movement covers 4 steps of ground. If you wanted the total ground covered per minute, would you add those numbers, or multiply them?

No wahala, here's a stronger hint: frequency (cycles per second) multiplied by wavelength (distance covered per cycle) gives distance covered per second, which is exactly speed — so the relationship has the shape v = f*λ. Try substituting f = 50 Hz and λ = 4 m into that yourself.
Sure — v = f*λ = 50*4 = 200 m/s. So the wave travels at 200 m/s, found simply by multiplying how many cycles pass per second by how far each cycle stretches.
phy-0037: Think of a talking drum beaten steadily during a dance, completing 4 beats every 2 seconds. How much time passes for JUST ONE beat, if 4 beats are spread evenly across 2 seconds?

Exactly — that's the time for one complete cycle, which is the period T. And frequency f is how many complete cycles happen per second — using f = number of oscillations/time, what do you get for frequency here?
Correct. Now compare your period (0.5 s) and frequency (2 Hz) — if you calculate 1/f, what do you get, and how does that relate to T?
phy-0093: Think about sending a message by okada to a neighbouring village and getting a reply back — the 2 seconds you measured is like the TOTAL time for the rider to go there AND come back, not just the one-way trip. If the round trip takes 2 seconds, how long did just the ONE-WAY journey to the wall take?
Correct. Now using distance = speed * time with the ONE-WAY time you just found, and the given speed of sound, what distance do you calculate to the wall?
phy-0041: Let's reason it through first. Think of a native flute open at both ends, versus the closed bottle you blow across. At BOTH open ends of the flute, is the air free to move (an antinode), or forced to stay still (a node)?

Fair, here's a stronger hint: with an antinode at BOTH ends instead of a node at one end, the shortest wave pattern that fits is HALF a full wave across the pipe's length, giving λ = 2*L instead of 4*L. Try that with v = f*λ.
Sure — λ = 2*L = 2*0.34 = 0.68 m. Then f = v/λ = 340/0.68 = 500 Hz. So the fundamental frequency is 500 Hz.
phy-0023: Think of a native flute that is open at both ends versus a bottle you blow across that is sealed at the bottom, closed at one end only. At the closed end of the bottle, can the air actually move freely back and forth, or is it forced to stay still there?

Fair, here's a stronger hint: because the closed end must be a node (no movement) and the open end must be an antinode (maximum movement), the shortest possible wave pattern that fits is only a QUARTER of a full wave inside the pipe's length L. That gives λ = 4*L. Try using v = f*λ with that.
Sure, step by step: λ = 4*L = 4*0.5 = 2 m. Then from v = f*λ, f = v/λ = 340/2 = 170 Hz. So the fundamental frequency is 170 Hz.
phy-0010: Think of water flowing through a narrow pipe from an overhead tank — the tank's height (pressure) pushes the water, and the pipe's narrowness resists the flow. In an electric circuit, which quantity plays the role of the 'pushing pressure', voltage or current?

Good. And current (3 A) is like the rate of water actually flowing through, being pushed by that pressure but held back by resistance. Ohm's law says V = I*R — if you know V and I, how would you rearrange this to solve for R?
Correct rearrangement. Now substitute V = 12 V and I = 3 A into R = V/I — what value do you get?
phy-0003: Think of two okada riders both carrying passengers from the same park to the same destination by two different roads at the same time, instead of one rider waiting for the other to finish first. Does opening a second road make the total trip for all passengers faster or slower overall?

Good — parallel paths make it EASIER for current to flow overall, meaning the combined resistance must be smaller than either resistor alone, not their simple sum. Does R = R1 + R2 = 10 ohm fit that idea of 'easier flow, smaller resistance'?
Right instinct. For parallel resistors, use 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Substitute R1 = 4 ohm and R2 = 6 ohm — what do you get for 1/R first, before inverting to find R?
phy-0043: Think of a village compound with one narrow single entrance gate leading into a courtyard that then splits into two separate paths to different buildings. Would you calculate the total 'resistance to movement' by treating everything as one big combined path all at once, or by first working out each independent section (the split paths) before combining with the single gate?
Exactly the right strategy. So first, treat the 3 ohm and 6 ohm resistors as the 'split paths' in parallel — using 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, what is their combined resistance?

Correct — the parallel section simplifies to 2 ohm. Now that 2 ohm parallel section is in series with the original 2 ohm resistor, like the single gate joined to the courtyard. How do you combine resistors in series, and what is the total resistance?
phy-0162: Think of a water vendor (mai ruwa) pushing his cart of jerrycans up a hill. Some of his strength is used just moving his own cart, before any water reaches your house. The battery also 'spends' some voltage pushing current through itself. What part of the battery causes that?
Exactly. The voltage used inside is the 'lost volts', I*r. What is I*r here?
Good. Now use V = E - I*r. What terminal voltage is available to the keke's lights and horn?
phy-0159: ₦6.3 million for ironing? Your mother would sell the iron! On a prepaid meter, the 'units' you buy are kilowatt-hours. Is 1500 W in watts or kilowatts, and what is it in kilowatts?
Right. Energy in kWh = power in kW * time in hours. How many hours in total is the iron used over the 30 days?
Exactly. Now, if each unit costs ₦70, what is the total cost of ironing for the month?
phy-0133: When you crank that windlass to bring up a bucket of water, your hand goes round a big circle while the rope winds round the small axle. In one complete turn, whose circle is longer — your hand's or the axle's?
Right. The distance round a circle is 2*π*r. So in one turn, effort moves 2*π*R and load rises 2*π*r. When you divide them to get VR, what happens to the 2*π?
Exactly. So what is the velocity ratio of the windlass, and what does it tell you about how far your hand moves compared with the bucket?
phy-0141: Remember the wheelbarrow boys at Mile 12 market. Everything turns about the wheel, so we measure every distance FROM the wheel's axle. Which distance is the load arm and which is the effort arm here?
Right. By the principle of moments, effort * effort arm = load * load arm. Write that out with the numbers.
Good. Solve for E. What effort must the boy apply at the handles, and what is the mechanical advantage of the wheelbarrow in this case?
phy-0130: Think of labourers lifting blocks up to the second floor with a pulley. MA tells you how many times the machine multiplies your FORCE. VR tells you how many times further your hand moves than the load. Which one depends on the forces 800 N and 250 N?

No problem — you've got the first part. MA = load/effort, so MA = 800/250. For efficiency, compare what you actually got (MA) with what an ideal, frictionless machine would give (VR): efficiency = (MA/VR)*100%. Try both steps.

Good instinct — efficiency can never exceed 100%, so the fraction was upside down. Step by step: MA = load/effort = 800/250 = 3.2. Efficiency = (MA/VR)*100% = (3.2/4)*100% = 0.8*100% = 80%. The missing 20% of the work goes into overcoming friction in the pulleys and lifting the lower pulley block and rope.
phy-0137: Think of it like a bus conductor: what the passengers pay is the input, what reaches the owner after 'settlements' is the output. Here, the labourer's work is the input. What work is actually done on the cement bag?
Good. And the input work is what the labourer does: his force times how far his hand moved. What is that?
Correct. Now efficiency = (work output/work input)*100%. What is the efficiency, to 1 decimal place, and where did the 'missing' 200 J go?
phy-0139: Think of a hand-pumped borehole in the village: if it is only 70% efficient, then out of every 100 units of effort you put in, only 70 come out as useful work lifting water. So would the machine's actual MA be equal to the VR of 5, or less than it?
Okay. Use efficiency = (MA/VR)*100%. Since efficiency is 70%, MA/VR = 0.7. So MA = 0.7*VR. Find MA first, then use MA = load/effort to get the effort.

You got MA right, just flip the last step. MA = load/effort, so effort = load/MA. Step by step: MA = 0.7*5 = 3.5. Effort = 1400/3.5 = 400 N. Check: MA = 1400/400 = 3.5, and (3.5/5)*100% = 70%. So the effort needed is 400 N — larger than the ideal 1400/5 = 280 N because of losses.
phy-0070: Recall the mason mixing cement — the energy for changing the block of ice from solid to liquid doesn't care what temperature it 'rises' to, because it doesn't rise at all during melting. So which two quantities in this question actually matter for the formula Q = m*L?
Correct. Now substitute the mass and the given specific latent heat into Q = m*L — what value do you get?
phy-0068: Imagine your mother is boiling water for tea — she doesn't just care what the water's starting temperature was, she cares how much hotter it needs to get. If the pot starts at 25°C and she wants it at 100°C, what single number tells you 'how much hotter'?
Right, that's Δθ. Now that you have Δθ, m and c all given, which formula links them, and what does it give you when you multiply all three together?
Good — go ahead and compute Δθ first, then finish the multiplication. What's your final value for Q, in joules?
phy-0067: Think about boiling water for two different sizes of pot on the same fire — a small pot of water and a big pot of water. Which one needs more firewood (more heat) to raise its temperature by the same amount?

Exactly — the heat needed depends on how much mass you're heating, not just the temperature change. So if Q = m*c*Δθ, and you already know Q, m and Δθ, which quantity are you solving for, and how would you rearrange the formula to make it the subject?
Correct rearrangement. Now work out Δθ first from the two temperatures given, then substitute all three values into c = Q/(m*Δθ) — what value do you get?
phy-0176: Think of the vulcanizer's foot pump. When he presses the pump down, the air inside is squeezed into a smaller space. Does it become easier or harder for him to push further — and what does that tell you about the pressure of the trapped air?
Exactly. For a fixed mass at constant temperature, Boyle's law says P_1*V_1 = P_2*V_2. Which values are P_1, V_1 and V_2 here?
Correct. Solve P_1*V_1 = P_2*V_2 for P_2. What is the new pressure, and how does halving the volume affect it?
phy-0177: Imagine a party balloon tied to a chair at an owambe in the hot afternoon. If the temperature goes from 27°C to 127°C, would the balloon really swell to almost five times its size? The gas laws only work if temperature is measured from absolute zero. Which temperature scale starts from absolute zero?
Yes, Kelvin — you've got it. Convert using T = θ + 273. So 27°C becomes 300 K and 127°C becomes 400 K. Then Charles's law says V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2. Put in V_1 = 300 cm^3 with the Kelvin values.

Let's finish it. 300/300 = 1, so 1 = V_2/400. Multiply both sides by 400: V_2 = 400 cm^3. So the volume rises from 300 cm^3 to 400 cm^3, not 1411 cm^3. The Kelvin temperature went up by a factor of 400/300 = 4/3, and so did the volume. Using Celsius gave a wrong ratio because 0°C is not zero energy.
phy-0150: Think of two water drums in a compound. The 'capacity' of a drum isn't how much water is in it now, but how much it holds per unit of 'filling pressure'. For a capacitor, capacitance is charge stored per volt. What operation gives you 'per volt'?
Exactly — C = Q/V, measured in farads (coulombs per volt). What do you get when you divide 60 μC by 12 V?
Right number. What is the unit — and what does that value mean about how much extra charge the capacitor would store for every extra volt?
phy-0148: Think of the price of tomatoes at the market. If a basket costs a certain amount, the price 'per kilogram' tells you what one kilogram costs. The field strength is like the 'price per coulomb' — the force on each coulomb of charge. What should you do with the total force and the charge to get force per coulomb?
Exactly — E = F/q, and its unit is N/C. So 0.02 N on its own is the force, not the field. Write down the division.
Correct. Work it out. What is the electric field intensity, with its unit?
phy-0147: Think of a rechargeable lantern in a dark room. When you move a book closer to the lantern, the light on the page doesn't just get a little stronger, it gets much brighter, because the light is spread over a smaller area. Coulomb's force behaves like that. Does it depend on r, or on r^2?
Fair enough. F = k*q_1*q_2/r^2, so F is proportional to 1/r^2. If r becomes r/2, then r^2 becomes (r/2)^2 = r^2/4. Dividing by something four times smaller makes F how many times bigger?

Yes, let's confirm step by step. F_new/F_old = (r_old/r_new)^2 = (r/(r/2))^2 = 2^2 = 4. So F_new = 4*0.8 = 3.2 N. You got 1.6 N because you treated F as proportional to 1/r instead of 1/r^2. Similarly, if the distance were doubled, the force would drop to 0.8/4 = 0.2 N.
phy-0146: That answer would be enough to throw a whole lorry off the Third Mainland Bridge — so something has gone wrong. First, a μC is a millionth of a coulomb, just like one kobo is a tiny part of a naira. Did you convert 2 μC and 3 μC to coulombs before multiplying?
Good. Now Coulomb's law is F = k*q_1*q_2/r^2. Note that r is SQUARED. What is r^2 here?
Correct. Now substitute everything: F = 9*10^9 * 2*10^-6 * 3*10^-6 / 0.09. What force do you get, and is it attractive or repulsive?
phy-0158: Think of sorting a family's ajo contribution: first you add up what the two sisters put together, then you deal with that combined amount as one. Which two capacitors form the 'sisters' group that you can combine first?
Good. Now that 6 μF acts as one capacitor in series with the 3 μF. Which rule do you use for series capacitors?
Correct. Solve for C, then use Q = C*V with 12 V. What is the total capacitance and the total charge drawn from the battery?
acc-0001: Think of an Esusu contribution book. When a member's money comes INTO the group's pool, the secretary writes it on one side; when money goes OUT to pay a member, it's written on the other side. In your transaction, which account is receiving something — Goods, or Cash?
Good. In accounting, the account that receives value is debited. So what happens to the Goods (Purchases) account?
Correct. Now, Cash left the business to pay for those goods — value is going OUT of the cash account. So what do we do to Cash?
Exactly. Now write both legs of this out as a single table with Date, Account, Debit and Credit columns, the way we always format it.
acc-0002: Think of a trader in the market who lets a trusted customer 'carry the goods now, pay next market day'. Has cash actually entered the trader's box today, or has something else of value been created — a promise to pay?

Exactly — that promise to pay is recorded as a debtor, in this case 'Chidi' or 'Debtors account', and since value (a right to receive money) has come INTO the business, what happens to that account — debit or credit?

Correct. Now the business gave OUT goods in exchange, meaning value left the Sales side conceptually — in accounting, a sale is recorded as income leaving through the Sales account. Which side does the Sales account go on, and can you now write both legs as a single table with Date, Account, Debit and Credit columns?
acc-0041: Think of a provisions store owner who takes three bags of rice from her own shop shelf for her family's kitchen at home, without paying herself any money for them. Has value still left the business, even though no cash was involved?

Exactly — drawings can be in goods, not just cash. Since these goods would otherwise have been available for sale (originally recorded in Purchases), which account should be reduced to reflect that these goods are no longer available for the business to sell?
Correct thinking. And the Drawings account records what the owner has taken out of the business, valued at cost. Can you lay both legs of this transaction out in our standard table format?
acc-0017: Think of a landlord who is owed ₦10,000 rent but tells the tenant, 'if you pay everything today in cash, I'll knock off ₦500 as a reward for prompt payment.' After the tenant pays ₦9,500, does the landlord still consider any part of the ₦10,000 still owing?

Exactly — the debt is fully cleared, but only ₦9,500 came in as cash; the other ₦500 is treated as an expense (discount allowed) to the business, not as unpaid debt. So to fully clear the debtor's ₦10,000 account, what two credit entries need to appear against it — cash of what amount, and discount allowed of what amount?

Good question to pause on — discount allowed is an expense to the business (money effectively lost), and expenses are debited. So the debtor's account is credited with both 9,500 (cash) and 500 (discount) to clear the full 10,000; can you now write out all three accounts affected — Debtor, Cash, and Discount Allowed — in our standard table?
acc-0059: Think of a market association's collector who gathers levies from traders on behalf of the local government, then hands that money over to the government office later. Does the collector treat the levy money as her own personal income, or as money she's simply holding to pass on to someone else?

Exactly the same idea with VAT — the business collects it from customers on behalf of the tax authority; it isn't the business's own revenue. So should the VAT portion of the ₦22,000 be included in Sales revenue, or kept separate as a liability owed to the tax authority?
Exactly right. If the ₦22,000 includes 10% VAT on top of the actual sale value, how would you work out the true Sales revenue figure (excluding VAT) from that ₦22,000?
acc-0013: Think of a compound house that is worth a certain amount in total. Some of that value was paid for using a loan from a cooperative society, and the rest was paid for from the family's own savings. If you know the total value of the house and how much is still owed on the loan, how would you find how much the family's own savings actually contributed?
Exactly that logic. In accounting, this is the accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Rearranged to find Capital, what would the formula be?
Correct rearrangement. Now substitute Assets = 300,000 and Liabilities = 120,000 — what is the owner's capital?
acc-0006: Think of a provisions store owner who started the month with some bags of rice already in the store, bought more bags during the month, and at month end counted what was still unsold. What she actually SOLD during the month is not just what she bought — it's what she started with, plus what she bought, minus what's left over. Does that logic make sense for finding what left the store?
Exactly — that's the cost of goods sold. Using opening stock + purchases − closing stock, what value do you get for cost of goods sold here?
Correct. Now, gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold — subtract your 125,000 from the ₦200,000 sales figure. What do you get?
acc-0010: Think of a trader's evening balance: her gross profit is like the pile of money already made from selling goods. Rent and wages are like money she has to pay OUT of that pile. But discount RECEIVED — money others gave HER as a reduction on what she owed them — does that come out of her pile, or add to it?

Exactly — discount received is other income, added to gross profit, not subtracted like an expense. So what is the correct order of operations: gross profit plus discount received, then minus the two expenses?
Correct approach. Work through that calculation — what is the final net profit figure?
acc-0022: Think of a yam seller who, from years of experience, knows that out of every 100 bags she sells on credit, roughly 5 bags' worth of money is never fully recovered from certain customers, even though she doesn't know in advance exactly WHICH customers will fail to pay. Should she wait until each failure actually happens before adjusting her expectations, or plan ahead using her experience?
Fair, here's the direct hint: the provision is simply an estimated percentage of total debtors, calculated as 5% of ₦80,000 — try that multiplication yourself first.

That's correct: 5% of 80,000 = ₦4,000. This means the business prudently reduces its expected recoverable debtors by ₦4,000 in the accounts (shown as a deduction from debtors in the balance sheet, and as an expense in the profit and loss account), reflecting realistic expectation of some unpaid debts even without knowing which specific customers will default.
acc-0097: Recall the firewood seller idea: to know the cost of what was actually SOLD (not just bought), you take opening stock plus purchases, then subtract what's left unsold (closing stock). What is the cost of sales using your opening stock, purchases, and closing stock figures?
Correct. Now find gross profit (Sales - Cost of sales), and then subtract the total expenses from gross profit to find net profit — what are your two final figures?
acc-0003: Think of a farmer who buys a wheelbarrow for ₦20,000, and after years of use, expects to sell the worn-out wheelbarrow for scrap metal at ₦2,000. Is the FULL ₦20,000 actually 'lost' to wear and tear, or only the part he won't recover at the end?
Exactly — depreciation only spreads out the amount actually lost in value, which is cost minus scrap (residual) value. So for the machine, what is that depreciable amount, cost minus scrap value?
Correct. Now divide that ₦90,000 depreciable amount evenly over the 5-year useful life — what is the annual depreciation charge?
acc-0030: Let's reason it out. Think of a worker hired exactly halfway through the month who is only paid for the days actually worked, not a full month's wages. Should the machine, which was only owned for half the year, be treated the same way for depreciation?

Fair, here's a stronger hint: first find the FULL year's depreciation as if it were owned all year (10% of 120,000), then take only half of that figure, since it was owned for exactly half the year. Try the first step yourself.
That's exactly right: full-year depreciation = 10% of 120,000 = 12,000. Since the machine was owned for only half the year, the actual charge for this year is half of that: 12,000/2 = ₦6,000.
acc-0008: Think of a farmer's yam barn that loses 20% of whatever is CURRENTLY inside it to spoilage every month, not 20% of the original full barn every time. If the barn already lost some yams last month, is this month's 20% spoilage calculated from the original full barn, or from what remains now?

Fair, here's a stronger hint: first find year one's depreciation as 20% of the original cost, subtract it to get the net book value at the start of year two, then take 20% of THAT reduced figure — not 20% of ₦500,000 again. Try working out year one's depreciation and the resulting net book value first.

Yes, let's finish it: year two's depreciation is 20% of the reduced net book value of ₦400,000, which is 0.20 * 400,000 = ₦80,000. Notice it's smaller than year one's ₦100,000, because reducing balance is always calculated on the shrinking net book value, not the original cost.
acc-0061: Let's build it year by year, like a farmer tracking how much yam remains in the barn after each month's consumption, where each month's consumption is a percentage of what's LEFT, not the original full barn. What is 25% of the original ₦200,000 for year one?
Fair, here's a stronger hint: for year two, apply 25% again, but to the NEW reduced balance of 150,000, not the original 200,000. Try that calculation yourself.

You're doing it correctly — 150,000 − 37,500 = ₦112,500. So after 2 years of reducing balance depreciation at 25%, the generator's net book value is ₦112,500, found by reapplying the rate to each year's reduced balance in turn.
acc-0100: Think about a farmer selling his old plough after years of use, for more than its estimated remaining worth. Is he running a 'plough-selling business' the way he runs his farming-produce-selling business, or is this a one-off event involving equipment he no longer needs?

Exactly — selling a fixed asset is not part of normal trading activity, so the ₦15,000 shouldn't be treated as sales revenue. Since the machine was sold for MORE than its book value, what would you call that ₦15,000 difference in the accounts?
acc-0012: Think of a village cooperative's bank agent who deducts a small service fee directly from the group's savings account, without first telling the group's own secretary who keeps the handwritten record book. Who finds out about that deduction first — the bank's own record, or the secretary's handwritten book?

Exactly — the bank statement is already correct and up to date on charges it applied; it's the cash book (the business's own record) that is missing this information and needs updating. So should you adjust the bank statement, or update your cash book to include the ₦500 charge?
Right. Since a bank charge reduces the money in the account, how would you record that ₦500 charge in the cash book — as an addition or a deduction from your cash book balance?
acc-0018: Think of dropping off a parcel at a village transport park just before the last vehicle leaves for the city — you know you've handed it over, but the receiver in the city won't confirm receiving it until the parcel actually arrives, maybe the next day. Has the parcel been lost, or is it simply still in transit?

Exactly right timing gap. Your cash book already shows the ₦15,000 as deposited, but the bank simply hasn't processed it into the statement yet. To reconcile, should you add or subtract this ₦15,000 on the bank statement side to bring it in line with your cash book?
Good — that's the correct adjustment direction. Once the bank processes it in the next statement period, will this difference still need adjusting, or will it disappear naturally?
acc-0004: Think of writing an IOU note to a friend at a village contribution meeting, promising to pay ₦7,000 from your Esusu savings — you've already recorded in your own book that the money is gone, but your friend hasn't yet gone to collect it from your savings box. At this moment, does your savings box actually show less money, or does it still show the full amount because the friend hasn't collected yet?

Exactly that timing gap. In the same way, you've already written the cheque and deducted it in your cash book, but the recipient hasn't yet presented it to the bank for payment, so the bank statement doesn't reflect it yet. To reconcile, do you adjust the bank statement balance by adding or subtracting the unpresented cheque to match your cash book logic?
Good instinct — try that subtraction with the figures given (₦52,000 bank balance, ₦7,000 unpresented cheque) and see whether it brings the two balances into agreement.
acc-0103: Think of a trader who happily recorded a customer's payment as received, only to later find out the customer's promise to pay was actually empty — the money never truly arrived in her purse. If she already recorded the money as received, but it turns out that never really happened, should her record stay as is, or does it need correcting?

Exactly right. Since the ₦18,000 was originally debited into the cash book (bank column) when the cheque was first received, and it turns out that money isn't really there, what entry would you now need to make to reverse that, and what happens to the customer's debtor balance as a result?
acc-0102: Let's reason from the bank statement's point of view. The unpresented cheque has already been deducted in YOUR cash book, but the bank hasn't deducted it yet since the supplier hasn't cashed it. So starting from the bank statement balance, should you add or subtract the unpresented cheque to reflect what the balance WILL become once the bank catches up?

Correct. Now for the ₦13,000 lodgement already recorded as received in YOUR cash book, but not yet appearing on the bank statement — should you add or subtract that from the bank statement balance to get it in line with your cash book?

Exactly right. Starting from the bank statement balance of ₦102,000, subtract the unpresented cheque and add the uncredited lodgement — what final adjusted balance do you get, and does it match the cash book balance of ₦85,000?
acc-0067: Think of two siblings who inherit a small family compound and decide to farm it together, but they never sat down to agree on how to split the harvest. If a dispute arises and there's no agreement in writing, would custom automatically favour whoever contributed more land, or would the community elders usually apply a simple, fair default like splitting it evenly?

That's exactly the logic accounting law follows too. When partners have NOT agreed on a profit-sharing ratio, what default rule do you think would apply, regardless of how much capital each partner contributed?
Exactly right. So for Musa and Tunde, without a partnership agreement specifying otherwise, how should this year's profit be divided between them, even though their capital contributions differ?
acc-0070: Think about dividing a basket of 5 equal-sized yams between two farmers, where one farmer gets 3 yams for every 2 the other gets. If you have exactly 5 yams to share this way, how many yams does each farmer receive?

No wahala, let's narrow it down: the ratio 3:2 has a TOTAL of 3+2 = 5 parts. Chidi's share is 3 out of those 5 parts (3/5 of the total), and Emeka's share is 2 out of 5 parts (2/5 of the total). What is 1 part worth, if the total profit of {N}100,000 is split into 5 equal parts?

Let's finish it together: if 1 part = ₦20,000, then Chidi (3 parts) gets 3*₦20,000 = ₦60,000, and Emeka (2 parts) gets 2*₦20,000 = ₦40,000. Check: ₦60,000 + ₦40,000 = ₦100,000, which matches the total net profit, confirming the split is correct.
acc-0072: Think of the basic double-entry idea: money coming INTO the business bank account is an increase in an asset (bank), and every increase in an asset needs a matching credit somewhere else. If Halima is contributing this cash as her OWN capital investment in the business, which account should be credited to show that the business now owes this amount to Halima as her stake?
Exactly right. So which account is debited (bank, since cash increased) and which is credited (Halima's capital account), and for what amount?
acc-0111: Let's separate what INCREASES Ibrahim's entitlement from what DECREASES it. Salary, interest on capital, and profit share are all amounts the business owes TO him for his contribution and work — would you expect these to be credited (increasing what's owed to him) or debited?

No wahala, let's narrow it down: drawings are money he has already TAKEN OUT of the business for himself, so they reduce what the business still owes him — drawings are DEBITED to his current account. So you need to ADD all the credit items (opening balance, salary, interest, profit share) and then SUBTRACT the debit item (drawings). What is the total of the credit items first?

Your addition is correct — let's finish it together: total credits = ₦95,000. Subtract the drawings (debit) of ₦50,000: ₦95,000 - ₦50,000 = ₦45,000. So Ibrahim's current account ends the year with a CREDIT balance of ₦45,000, meaning the business still owes him that amount, which would typically be carried forward or paid out.
acc-0069: Think of sharing the proceeds from a joint family farm: before splitting the remaining harvest equally between two siblings, you'd first set aside a portion to pay the sibling who did extra work (like a labourer's wage) and reward each based on how much seed money they invested. Which items in this question look like they should be set aside FIRST, before the equal split happens?

Exactly the right order. So starting from the {N}200,000 net profit, what is left over (the residual profit) after deducting Ade's {N}40,000 salary and the total interest on capital of {N}20,000 + {N}10,000?

Correct arithmetic. Since that {N}130,000 residual is shared EQUALLY between Ade and Bola, how much residual profit does each partner get, and what is each partner's TOTAL share once you add back their own salary and interest on capital?
acc-0126: Suppose your town union's purse had some money in January, and during the year the union spent more on the chief's reception than it collected in levies. Did the purse get fuller or emptier?

No problem, let's make it concrete. A deficit means expenditure was MORE than income — the union used up some of its old savings to cover the gap. So the deficit REDUCES the fund. Try the calculation again using subtraction: ₦180,000 minus the deficit.

Let's check it the long way. Suppose income was ₦100,000 and expenditure ₦122,000 — that's a deficit of ₦22,000. The union had to take ₦22,000 from its savings to pay the extra bills. So the accumulated fund falls: ₦180,000 − ₦22,000 = ₦158,000. A surplus is added to the fund; a deficit is deducted.
acc-0113: Think of the town union treasurer's cash box. On the first day of the year she opened it and there was already ₦45,000 inside, left over from last year. Then money came in and money went out. If you only compare what came in with what went out this year, have you accounted for everything that is in the box?

No wahala, let me narrow it. Your ₦40,000 is correct as the EXCESS of receipts over payments for the year. But the box didn't start empty. The receipts and payments account always opens with the balance b/d. So the closing figure = balance at start + total receipts − total payments. What is ₦45,000 + ₦205,000 − ₦165,000?

Let's lay it out together. Balance b/d ₦45,000. Add receipts: ₦120,000 + ₦30,000 + ₦55,000 = ₦205,000, so cash available = ₦250,000. Less payments: ₦60,000 + ₦25,000 + ₦80,000 = ₦165,000. Closing cash balance c/d = ₦250,000 − ₦165,000 = ₦85,000. Your ₦40,000 was the year's net inflow; adding the ₦45,000 the treasurer started with gives the ₦85,000 she should find in the box.
acc-0128: Think of an okada rider who pays his owner weekly. In January he paid off ₦8,000 he owed from December, and at the end of this year he still owes the last ₦6,000. If you want to know what the bike hire for THIS year really cost him, is it just the total cash he handed over?
Right. So which of the two figures, ₦8,000 and ₦6,000, do you remove from ₦40,000, and which do you add?
Exactly. And where does the ₦6,000 owing appear in the club's balance sheet?
acc-0115: Think of an Aso-ebi coordinator for a 2024 wedding. Some people paid in 2024 for LAST year's wedding they owed, some paid in 2024 for next year's wedding, and some who wore this year's fabric haven't paid yet. If you want to know how much was really earned from THIS year's wedding, which of those three groups would you remove, and which would you add back?
Now translate that directly to the association's dues. Start from ₦80,000 and apply those three adjustments. What figure do you get?

Correct. Here is how the subscriptions account proves your ₦79,000; the income figure is the balancing item:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (arrears) | 5,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 80,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 79,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in advance) | 3,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in arrears) |  | 7,000 |
|  | Total | 87,000 | 87,000 |
Which of the two closing balances would you show as a current asset in the balance sheet, and which as a current liability?
acc-0117: Think of the social club like a gym at the end of the street. At the start of the year, some members owed old fees (the gym is owed), and some had prepaid (the gym owes them this year's service, which it will now deliver). Which of those two opening groups gives the gym MORE income to recognise this year without new cash coming in?

I hear you, it's a lot at once. One step: the ₦2,500 paid in advance LAST year is membership being enjoyed THIS year, so it is added to this year's income. The ₦4,000 opening arrears was last year's income being collected now, so it is taken OUT of this year's cash. Try: ₦96,000 − ₦4,000 + ₦2,500, then handle the two closing figures the opposite way. What do you get?

Let's finish it with the account itself:
| Date | Account | Debit (₦) | Credit (₦) |
|------|---------|-----------|------------|
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (arrears) | 4,000 |  |
| 1 Jan | Balance b/d (in advance) |  | 2,500 |
| 31 Dec | Cash |  | 96,000 |
| 31 Dec | Income and Expenditure | 97,000 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in advance) | 3,500 |  |
| 31 Dec | Balance c/d (in arrears) |  | 6,000 |
|  | Total | 104,500 | 104,500 |
Reading it: closing arrears (₦6,000) is this year's income not yet received, so it is added; closing advance (₦3,500) is cash for next year, so it is removed. ₦94,500 + ₦6,000 − ₦3,500 = ₦97,000, the balancing figure transferred to the income and expenditure account.
bece-eng-u1-l1: Imagine you are at the bus stop and someone says the danfo 'moved slowly'. Is 'slowly' telling us about the bus itself, or about how it moved?
Now look at our sentence. Which word is the action Ada did? And which word tells us the manner in which she did it?
Remember the rule: words describing nouns are adjectives, but words describing verbs (how, when, where) belong to a different group. Many of them end in '-ly'. Which group fits?
bece-eng-u1-l2: Picture your class prefect saying: 'Each student will bring one broom.' Is the prefect talking about the students as a group, or about every single student one by one?
In our sentence, 'of the boys' is only extra information. Cover it with your finger. What word is left as the subject?
A singular subject needs a singular verb, just like 'He ___ a book' or 'She ___ a pen'. Read each option with 'Each' alone and pick the one that sounds right for one person.
bece-eng-u1-l3: Think of two people at a party. One shares jollof rice with everybody; the other hides his plate and shares with nobody. Which one is generous?
Now, the question wants the OPPOSITE. One of the options means almost the same thing as generous. Can you spot it and remove it?
Being rich or humble is not about sharing at all. Look for the word that describes the person who hides his plate.
bece-eng-u1-l4: Imagine NEPA took light and you used a lantern to do your homework. When the light finally came back, was the homework already done or not yet started?
'Restored' is past tense. So we need a verb form that shows an action completed even EARLIER in the past. Which options are present or future? Remove them.
English uses 'had' + past participle for the action that happened first when two past actions are compared. Look for that pattern among the options.
bece-eng-u1-l5: If your friend Ngozi owns a bag, do we write Ngozi's bag or Ngozis' bag? How many people own the mother in our sentence?
Remove any option where the apostrophe is missing or placed after the 's'. Which options are left?
In a list like 'yam, egg and bread', commas go between the items, never between the verb and the first item. Check where each comma falls in the remaining options.
bece-sci-u1-l1: Think of a cold zobo ice block a seller puts in her cooler. After some hours in the hot sun, what do you find at the bottom of the cooler?
So the ice went from solid to liquid. Evaporation is liquid to gas, and condensation is gas to liquid. Can you rule those out?
Freezing goes from liquid to solid, the opposite direction. Which remaining word names the change from solid to liquid?
bece-sci-u1-l2: When NEPA takes light, you grab your torch. Before you press the switch, is the battery giving out any light or sound?
So light is what the energy becomes AFTER switching on, not how it is stored. Kinetic energy is for moving things. Is the battery moving?
Food and firewood also store energy in the substances they are made of, which is released by reactions. Batteries work the same way. Which option names that type of stored energy?
bece-sci-u1-l3: Think of your school: some students carry messages, some sweep, and the security man guards the gate. Blood also has parts with different jobs. Which job are we looking for?
Red blood cells carry oxygen, like messengers. Platelets help blood clot when you cut your finger. So neither of them is the guard. What is left?
Plasma is the liquid that carries dissolved food and the cells. The guard must be a type of cell. Which cell in the list have we not yet given a job?
bece-sci-u1-l4: Picture a labourer at a building site pushing sand in a wheelbarrow. Where is the turning point, where is the sand, and where do his hands lift?
Lever classes are named by what sits in the middle. If the fulcrum is in the middle (like a see-saw), that is one class. Here, what is in the middle?
Remember: fulcrum in the middle, load in the middle, or effort in the middle give the three classes in order 1, 2, 3. Match the wheelbarrow to that list.
bece-sci-u1-l5: Pushing a cart one metre is hard work. Pushing it across the whole market is MORE work. So does more distance give you more or less work?
Pushing harder also means more work. So work grows when force grows AND when distance grows together. Which operation makes a number grow with both of them?
The formula is Work = Force x Distance, measured in joules (J). Put in Emeka's numbers and calculate carefully.
bece-bus-u1-l1: Think of the business centre near your school where people go before exams. What do they usually go there to do with their documents?
A stapler joins sheets together, and a perforator punches holes for files. Do either of these make new copies?
A franking machine prints postage marks on envelopes. Which remaining machine reproduces a page many times?
bece-bus-u1-l2: Tomato lorries travel from the North to Mile 12 market in Lagos every day. Did those lorries cross into another country?
Foreign trade is between two countries, and entrepot trade is importing goods only to re-export them. Do either fit a journey inside Nigeria?
Barter means swapping goods without money, but our trader buys and sells. Which remaining option describes trade within one country?
bece-bus-u1-l3: Imagine an okada rider sells you a helmet that breaks the first time it falls. What should that helmet have done for you?
In Mama Bisi's case, she was free to choose what to buy, so choice was not the problem. What was the actual harm to her family?
Each consumer right protects something: freedom to pick, a voice to complain, knowledge, or protection from harm. Which one matches people falling sick?
bece-bus-u1-l4: Think of an Esusu collector with a notebook. When members bring money, he writes it on one side; when he pays someone out, he writes on the other. Why keep them apart?
In bookkeeping, the left side of the cash book is for money coming IN and the right side is for money going OUT. Is a receipt coming in or going out?
Each side of the cash book has its own name, and you met both names in class. Remember which side money coming IN goes to, what is that side called?
bece-bus-u1-l5: Imagine your mum gives you some money for the market. Someone then pays you back what they owed, and you spend some on a keke ride. Does the keke fare increase or reduce what is in your pocket?
So the opening cash and the sales money both come IN, and the transport money goes OUT. Which numbers do you add, and which do you subtract?
Use: Closing balance = Opening cash + Receipts - Payments. Put in Chidi's three figures and work it out step by step.
ncee-mat-u1-l1: Imagine Mama Bisi counts naira notes in bundles: single notes, bundles of ten, bundles of hundred. Each place in a number is like a different bundle. Can you name the places from the right?
Good! The 5 is in the units place and the 8 is in the tens place. Which place does the 3 sit in?
Keep walking left one more step past the hundreds place. What is that place called, and how many of them does 7 stand for?
ncee-mat-u1-l2: Picture 12 puff-puff on a tray, and Ada wants to share them equally among 4 plates. What does the 4 at the bottom of 1/4 tell you?
Right, it tells you how many equal plates. If you share 12 puff-puff onto 4 plates, how many go on each plate?
Ada only ate what is on ONE plate. So divide 12 by 4 and that is your answer. Be careful not to count what is left over!
ncee-mat-u1-l3: When a market woman gives you 'discount', do you pay more or less than the first price?
Correct, less! Now, 10% means 10 out of every 100. How many hundreds are in ₦2,000, and what is 10 naira for each of them?
Once you know how much the discount is in naira, take it away from ₦2,000. Don't stop at the discount itself, that's not what you pay!
ncee-mat-u1-l4: Imagine one danfo leaves the park every 4 minutes and another every 6 minutes. They both leave at the start. After how many minutes will they leave together again?
Let's list the times: the first danfo leaves at 4, 8, ... and the second at 6, ... Can you continue both lists for a few more numbers?
Look for the FIRST number that appears in both lists. Remember, LCM is the lowest one they share, not just 4 × 6, and not a number that divides them.
ncee-mat-u1-l5: If you wanted to cover the whole garden with square mats, 1 m by 1 m each, would you be counting the space inside or walking round the fence?
Yes, the space inside! Imagine 5 rows of mats, and each row has 8 mats. How can you find the total number of mats quickly?
Multiply length by width. Be careful: adding all the sides gives the perimeter, which is a different thing.
ncee-eng-u1-l1: Most words just add -s, like one mango, two mangoes, or one book, two books. But some words are special. Can you think of the plural of 'man' or 'woman'?
Nice, 'men' and 'women' change inside instead of adding -s. 'Child' is one of these special words too. What does the headmaster call all the pupils at assembly: 'Good morning, ...'?
Remember: a special plural is already plural, so it does not need an extra -s on top. Which option sounds like the word your teacher uses?
ncee-eng-u1-l2: Imagine your friend shares his puff-puff with everyone at break time. We call him generous. What kind of person would hide his puff-puff and share with nobody?
Good thinking. Now, a kind person and a generous person are quite similar, aren't they? So would 'kind' be the opposite, or a word that means almost the same?
Also, being rich or happy is not about sharing. Look for the word that describes someone who refuses to share.
ncee-eng-u1-l3: Which word in the sentence tells us WHEN Tunde made the trip to the market, is it today, tomorrow or a day that has passed?
Yes, 'yesterday' means the past. Which options are for now? 'I go' and 'he goes' are for things happening now or every day. So we can cross those out.
Now between the two past-looking words: one needs a helper like 'has' or 'have' before it. Tunde has no helper word here, so pick the one that stands alone.
ncee-eng-u1-l4: Have you heard the spelling rhyme: 'i before e, except after c'? What letter comes just before the 'ie' or 'ei' in this word?
Yes, the letter c! So after c, should the e come first or the i come first?
Also check the start of the word: the sound 'see' here is made with the letter c, not s. Find the option that follows both clues.
ncee-eng-u1-l5: When you write your name on your exercise book, how do you start it, with a big letter or a small letter? Sentences are the same way. Which options start correctly?
Good. Now, this sentence is ASKING something, like when Mama asks 'Have you eaten?'. What mark do we put at the end of a question?
Last check: the bag belongs to Emeka, so we need a small mark called an apostrophe before the s. Pick the option that gets all three right.
ncee-sci-u1-l1: Think about things in your compound. Does a goat eat? Does a chicken lay eggs and have chicks? Those are signs of living things.
What about the mango tree, does it grow bigger every year and make new mangoes with seeds? So is a tree living or non-living?
Now look for the one thing that never eats, never grows and never has young ones, no matter how long you wait.
ncee-sci-u1-l2: When your mother waters the vegetables in the garden, where does she pour the water, on top of the leaves or on the soil?
Right, on the soil! So the part that drinks the water must be touching the soil. Which parts of a plant are up in the air, and which part is hidden underground?
Leaves, flowers and fruits are all above the ground. Choose the part that grips the soil and holds the plant firmly.
ncee-sci-u1-l3: Imagine you played football in the sand at break time. Your hands look clean, but tiny germs are on them. Can you see germs with your eyes?
No, germs are too small to see! So waiting until hands look or smell dirty is not safe. How do germs from your hands get inside your body?
Think about when you pick up your rice, eba or puff-puff with your fingers. Which option protects you at that moment?
ncee-sci-u1-l4: Before Bisi put the water in, was it a liquid you could pour? And after, was it a hard solid? So water changed from what to what?
Good, liquid to solid. Melting is when ice cream left in the sun turns soft and runny. Is that the same direction or the opposite?
Boiling and evaporation need heat, like water on the stove becoming vapour. Bisi used cold, not heat. Look for the word that matches the cold machine she used.
ncee-sci-u1-l5: When you and your friend play on a see-saw, one side goes up while the other goes down. What is the see-saw resting on in the middle?
That middle point is called a pivot or fulcrum. Does a see-saw have a rope going over a wheel, or a sloping ramp? So which options can you rule out?
A simple machine made from a stiff bar turning on a fulcrum is the same kind you use when you open a bottle of malt with an opener. Which option names it?
